Q: Bash function: redirect command output to file but keep function printf output on stdout A:

Re-reading your question, It seem you just need to use STDERR for terminal output:

execute_command_with_progress_bar() {
    printf "START\n" >&2
    "$@" &

    local pid="$!"
    printf "LOOP\n" >&2

    while kill -0 "$pid" 2> /dev/null; do
        printf "o" >&2
        sleep 1
    done

    printf "END\n" >&2
}

If you want to store output AND print them to terminial, you have to multiply them.

Having a function that permit both redirections of STDERR and STDOUT

And still output something on terminal, as your comment request for

For this, you have to open another file descriptor which point to STDOUT,

Consider this

# bash source file for defining "execute_command_with_progress_bar" function

[[ $__execProgressFD ]] && [[ -t $__execProgressFD  ]] ||
    exec {__execProgressFD}>&1

execute_command_with_progress_bar() {
    printf "START\n" >&$__execProgressFD
    "$@" &

    local pid="$!"
    printf "LOOP\n" >&$__execProgressFD

    while kill -0 "$pid" 2> /dev/null; do
        printf "o" >&$__execProgressFD
        sleep 1
    done
    wait $pid
    printf "END\n" >&$__execProgressFD
}

Then:

$ . exec_progress.sh 
$ execute_command_with_progress_bar >/tmp/testfile.log 2>&1 \
    sh -c "sleep 2;ls -ld /tmp /tnt;sleep 2"
START
LOOP
ooooEND

$ cat /tmp/testfile.log 
[1] 2228115
ls: cannot access '/tnt': No such file or directory
drwxrwxrwt 41 root root 868352 Mar  9 12:17 /tmp
[1]+  Done                    "$@"

Or this for a real spinner...

# bash source file for defining "execute_command_with_spinner" function

[[ $__execProgressFD ]] && [[ -t $__execProgressFD  ]] ||
    exec {__execProgressFD}>&1

__execProgressSpinnerShapes=(  ⢎\   ⠎⠁  ⠊⠑  ⠈⠱  \ ⡱  ⢀⡰  ⢄⡠  ⢆⡀  )

execute_command_with_spinner() {
    printf "START\n" >&$__execProgressFD
    "$@" &

    local pid="$!" pnt
    printf "LOOP\e[?25l\n" >&$__execProgressFD # cursor invisible
    while kill -0 "$pid" 2> /dev/null; do
    # Save cursor position, render frame, restore cursor position
        printf >&$__execProgressFD '\e7%b\e8' \
           "${__execProgressSpinnerShapes[pnt++ %
                   ${#__execProgressSpinnerShapes[@]}]}"
    read -rsn 1 -t .05 _
    done
    wait $pid
    printf "\e[?25h\rEND\n" >&$__execProgressFD # cursor visible
}

Note: if running under GNU/Linux, you'd better use /proc pseudo file system instead of running a fork to kill for each loop. Replace kill -0 by:

    while [[ -d /proc/$pid ]]; do

But if you want to store output while printing them

For this, you could use tee command:

logfile="path/to/logfile.log"
exec 1> >(tee /dev/tty >>"$logfile")

Then everything sent to STDOUT will be added to $logfile and send to current terminal at same time.

More samples and infos at

  • How to redirect and append both standard output and standard error to a file with Bash
  • Pipe into many processes

Q: How do let and case differ in terms of lazyness? A:

Is that last snippet the alternative code that Marlow alludes to? If not, what is it?

Yes, that's the right snippet to compare to.

Why using case should cause an eager evaluation of the whole list reverse ys? Where do I read this myself? In C++, I try to read the standard draft, but what about Haskell? Is it this one?

Yes, the Haskell Report is the canonical specification. (But see also the "Known Bugs and Infelicities -> Haskell standards vs. Glasgow Haskell: language non-compliance" section of the GHC manual.) The relevant paragraph of the Report for case is in section 3.13:

A case expression is evaluated by pattern matching the expression e against the individual alternatives. The alternatives are tried sequentially, from top to bottom.

The (implied) consequence of this is that the scrutinee must be evaluated far enough to know if an alternative matches. This won't in general require a full evaluation, but this case is special: it calls reverse, whose definition is given in section 9.1, and which does not produce its first constructor until it has processed the entire spine of its input.

The relevant paragraph for let is in section 3.12, and makes the difference abundantly clear:

The dynamic semantics of the expression let { d1 ; … ; dn } in e0 are captured by this translation: ...

let p = e1 in e0 = case e1 of ~p -> e0 where no variable in p appears free in e1

The ~ in the case translation makes the match lazy.

I've tried using :sprint (which I've seen for the first time reading this book, after 5 years since my first contact with Haskell, believe it or not) to experiment with let and case and work out the answer, but I haven't come up with anything senseible.

Here's a short ghci transcript demonstrating the difference.

> x = "abcde"
> case reverse x of _:_ -> ()
()
> :sprint x
x = "abcde" -- actually, this is an optimization; the spec only requires [_, _, _, _, _]
> x = "abcde"
> let _:_ = reverse x in ()
()
> :sprint x
x = _ -- not yet evaluated

let x = … in … is a let expression, right? But what is let x = … in a do expression called?

If I needed to draw this distinction, I would name it a let statement.

Q: Stratified Sampling with Pyspark Multiples Columns A:

You can use the sampleBy method for pyspark DataFrames to perform stratified sample and pass the column name and a dictionary for the fractions within each column. For example:

spark_df.sampleBy("OCCUPA_ID", fractions={"2705": 0.7, "2708": 0.2, "2712": 0.1}, seed=42).show()

+------+---------+---------+
|CLI_ID|OCCUPA_ID|DIG_LABEL|
+------+---------+---------+
|     1|     2705|        7|
|     4|     2705|        1|
|     5|     2705|        7|
|     7|     2708|        2|
|    12|     2705|        1|
|    16|     2708|        2|
|    18|     2708|        2|
|    20|     2705|        7|
|    25|     2705|        2|
|    26|     2705|        2|
|    38|     2705|        7|
|    40|     2705|        1|
|    44|     2705|        2|
|    48|     2708|        7|
|    50|     2708|        2|
|    53|     2705|        1|
|    57|     2705|        1|
|    58|     2712|        1|
|    61|     2705|        2|
|    63|     2708|        7|
+------+---------+---------+
only showing top 20 rows

Since you want one pyspark DataFrame with two samplings performed from two different columns, you can chain the sampleBy methods together:

spark_stratified_sample_df = spark_df.sampleBy("OCCUPA_ID", fractions={"2705": 0.7, "2708": 0.2, "2712": 0.1}, seed=42).sampleBy("DIG_LABEL", fractions={"1": 0.5, "2": 0.2, "7": 0.3}, seed=42)

Q: ImagePullBackOff error because of DNS resolve problem A:

The nslookup command shows that DNS Server is "10.41.128.98". but why pod log says like "lookup my.docker.proxy.com on [2001:100:100:11::a]:53: server misbehaving;"? It seems like DNS server is "[2001:100:100:11::a]".

A system can have multiple DNS servers configured – and it's very common to have the same DNS server via both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

When you have multiple DNS server addresses, usually programs will try them in some specific order. The error message looks like it came from a Golang program, and I don't know what Golang does exactly, but I believe it queries all the OS-configured servers until gets an answer – much like the DNS functions in the OS itself.

Nslookup differs in this regard, and always uses only the first server that was configured. So for example, if your OS has both 10.41.128.98 and 2001:100:100:11::a configured, then the OS will use both servers, but nslookup will always use the first one unless told otherwise.

And secondly, Why nslookup command shows "** server can't find my.docker.proxy.com: REFUSED", even though it already show 'my.docker.proxy.com' address is 10.251.186.33?

That's because nslookup actually makes two DNS queries – one for A records, one for AAAA records (IPv4 and IPv6 addresses respectively) – and the incompetently written DNS server at 10.41.128.98 returns an error code for the 2nd query instead of just returning an empty response.

(Maybe it's an internal proxy that is trying to block IPv6?)

According to the clarification in RFC 8906 (section 7), a nameserver is not allowed to refuse queries based on the type alone. The nameserver's "authority" is for the whole domain name, so either it handles all queries for a specific domain (and/or from a specific client) or it doesn't, but it cannot handle some types and still return 'REFUSED' for some other types.

If the server recognizes the requested name but doesn't have any data about the specific type (e.g. if the name genuinely has no IPv6 AAAA records), the correct response would be a success reply with 0 records of that type. By returning a valid answer for one type and 'REFUSED' for the other, the nameserver is contradicting itself by saying that it allows requests for that domain name and that it doesn't accept them, so the "Server misbehaving" error message is true.
